reconcile.connective: Commentators answer that "son of God" is not one title but several senses — Christ's by nature, Adam's by creation, believers' by adoption — so the uses do not compete.

discrepancy.connective: The objection is pressed by Steve Wells, who catalogues the title's incompatible uses — Jesus the "only begotten," yet Adam and Spirit-led believers also "sons of God" — as a single inconsistency.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "How many sons does God have?"
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (2013), "How many sons does God have?"

excerpts.excerpt_text: they are the sons of God: not in so high a sense as Christ is; nor in so low a sense as Adam was, and angels are; much less in such sense as wicked magistrates be; nor merely as professors of religion in common; but by adoption, not national, such as that of the Jews, but special …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the whole tension in one sentence: distinguishes believers' sonship from Christ's ('not in so high a sense'), from Adam's ('not in so low a sense'), classing them as sons 'by adoption' — exactly the three overlapping uses the question pits against each other.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Adam was the son of God: Adam had no earthly father since God created him. … Adam, the first son of God, failed when tested, but Jesus, the Son of God in the fullest sense, successfully resisted temptation.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Distinguishes Adam's sonship (by creation, no earthly father) from Jesus' sonship 'in the fullest sense,' directly addressing how Luke 3:38 and the 'only begotten' texts can both stand. Two sentences from the same note joined by a sense-preserving ellipsis.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Romans 8:14
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this passage directly, expressly distinguishing the senses in which Christ, Adam, and believers are each called 'son of God' — the harmonizing answer to the multiple-uses objection.
